messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

As a firefighter, Alessandro had always been drawn to high-pressure situations, but nothing could have prepared him for the trauma he experienced as a relief worker in a war-torn country. The memories of that time still lingered, and he often found himself on edge, even in the safety of his own home. He would catch himself scanning the exits whenever he entered a room, a habit he had developed to ensure his own survival in the midst of chaos. Alessandro's wife, Rachel, had grown concerned about the changes she saw in him since his return from the war zone. She noticed that he avoided exercise, which had once been an integral part of his daily routine as a firefighter. When she asked him why, Alessandro confessed that it made him feel too vulnerable, too exposed. He also found himself pushing away positive emotions, as if allowing himself to feel happy or content would somehow make him less prepared for the dangers that lurked around every corner. As he navigated his daily routine, Alessandro couldn't shake off the feeling of being on guard. Even in ordinary situations, he felt threatened by strangers approaching him – a colleague's friendly greeting at the fire station could send his heart racing. His eyes would dart towards the exits, mentally mapping out escape routes as if danger was always just one step behind. Rachel tried to reassure him that they were safe, but Alessandro knew what it was like to have your world turned upside down in an instant. Alessandro's strategies for coping with these feelings – avoiding exercise and positive emotions, staying close to exits – had become second nature to him. But as he went about his day, he began to realize that these habits were not alleviating his sense of threat; they were actually feeding it. The more he avoided certain situations or emotions, the more his mind seemed to dwell on the potential dangers lurking within them. At work, Alessandro's colleagues had started to notice a change in him too. He was always one step ahead, anticipating every possible scenario, but this heightened state of alertness came at a cost. His relationships with his team members began to suffer as he struggled to connect with them on anything other than a superficial level. It wasn't until Alessandro received a commendation for his bravery in the line of duty that he finally broke down and told Rachel about the depth of his fears. He had always prided himself on being able to handle whatever came his way, but this time, something inside him snapped. As they hugged each other tightly, Alessandro realized that he couldn't keep living like this – constantly scanning for threats, avoiding life's joys in case they made him feel vulnerable. With Rachel's support, Alessandro began to consider seeking help, hoping that therapy could teach him how to quiet his mind and learn to trust the world around him again. He knew it wouldn't be easy, but he was tired of living in a state of perpetual alertness, tired of letting fear dictate every move he made.
